18: USERRA discrimination claim: whether Miller's non-selection was motivated by his military service or disabled veteran status; Board's finding of no discrimination upheld as supported by substantial evidence
we find that substantial evidence supports the ultimate conclusion that Dr. Miller failed to meet his burden of proof.
129: Disability discrimination and reprisal contentions did not supply a basis to overturn removal based on loss of security clearance; Egan limits the Board's inquiry, so the agency prevailed.
In any event, we see no error in the Board's determination that such contentions supply no basis for overturning the removal based on loss of a job-required security clearance.
411: USERRA violation as affirmative defense: Congress withheld judicial review of USERRA reemployment determinations at FBI, so the Board's dismissal of the defense affirmed
Congress intended to exclude the substantive determination from judicial review of any kind, including when presented in the context of an affirmative defense under 5 U.S.C. § 7701(c)(2).
414: Discrimination claim (age, race, sex, etc.) under the Congressional Accountability Act: the complaint did not state a discrimination claim because no facts plausibly showed the garnishment was based on protected status.
On its face, the complaint filed under 2 U.S.C. § 1405 does not allege that the Department's actions were based on race or age discrimination.
624: USERRA discrimination claim: Price failed to carry his initial burden of showing military service was a substantial or motivating factor in his non-selection for the General Engineer and Project Manager vacancies; dual announcements not per se discriminatory.
We find no error in the conclusions by the Board and the administrative judge that Mr. Price failed to provide any evidence to carry his initial burden.
625: VEOA veterans' preference claim: simultaneous use of competitive and merit promotion procedures is not itself a violation, and Price received the bona fide opportunity to compete he was due under VEOA; no numerical rating bonus in merit promotion.
Under VEOA, “[a]n agency’s simultaneous use of the competitive process and the merit promotion process is not of itself a violation of veterans preference.”
778: VEOA claim that the FDIC failed to credit Miller's military and other experience under 5 U.S.C. § 3311(2) and 5 C.F.R. § 302.302(d) in the non-selection; the court held no VEOA violation was shown on the modified reasoning that the Board must ensure experience was actually considered.
We discern no reversible error in the Board's ruling that a VEOA violation was not shown.
812: Whether USPS was required to accommodate the employee's disability by reassigning him to a part-time or newly created position; the court held no accommodation was available and the agency need not create a position.
to the extent that Thibeault does argue that USPS should have created a new position for him to accommodate his disability, the AJ correctly determined that USPS was not required to do so.
895: VEOA veterans' preference: whether HHS properly evaluated Jones's experience and found him not qualified for the PHA positions, with credit owed for military and other valuable experience.

Because the Board's findings are supported by substantial evidence, and because we are not free at this stage to reweigh the credibility determinations made below, we must uphold the Board's determination regarding the agency's evaluation of Mr. Jones's qualifying experience.
897: Age discrimination claim: whether Jones was passed over because of his age; court found he was not selected because he was deemed unqualified.
the record demonstrates that he was passed over for the PHA positions because he was deemed unqualified, not because of his age.
919: VEOA veterans' preference claim: whether 5 U.S.C. § 3304(f)(1)'s term 'agency' means the DOD (parent department) or the subcomponent DCMA, and whether OPM's regulation defining 'agency' as an executive agency under 5 U.S.C. § 105 is a permissible Chevron construction entitled to controlling weight.
An agency regulation that adopts as its own a relevant definition from the governing statutory scheme does not “manifestly contra[dict]” the statute.
972: USERRA discrimination claim: whether Grayton's military service was a motivating factor in his nonselection for a Claims Specialist position; Board found no discrimination and the court affirmed under substantial evidence review.
Accordingly, we affirm the Board's decision.
1084: EEO retaliation affirmative defense; the Board found Hansen failed to prove a genuine nexus between her EEO activity and her removal.
Ms. Hansen failed to meet her burden of proving retaliation by a preponderance of the evidence.
1108: VEOA veterans' preference claim: VA deemed preference-eligible applicant ineligible for GS-14 position for lack of specialized experience; Board correctly denied corrective action because VEOA does not let veterans be considered for positions for which they are not qualified and does not empower the Board to supplant VA criteria.
As we have stated, the VEOA does not enable veterans to be considered for positions for which they are not qualified.
1110: VEOA claim regarding HHS/CDC competitive selection announcements: HHS made all selections from concurrent merit promotion announcements Jones did not apply to, which did not violate VEOA; Board correctly denied corrective action.

an agency may solicit applications from both the public and merit promotion applicants simultaneously, and then fill the vacant position from the merit promotion certificate without violating the rights of those who applied only through the public, competitive process.
1153: Veterans' preference under VEOA: whether the agency's qualification assessment of the preference-eligible veteran and the inapplicability of the rule of three and pass-over requirements were lawful
Substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that the DVA complied with this order.
1203: USERRA discrimination claim: employee failed to show military service was a substantial or motivating factor in his resignation; AJ credibility findings upheld
Thus, Mr. Corbin has failed to demonstrate error in the Final Decision.
1294: USERRA discrimination claim: whether military service was a motivating factor in denial of tour extension and whether the agency proved it would have made the same decision anyway

We conclude that the evidence permits only one reasonable finding: the evidence establishes the presence of all four of the Sheehan factors, which together demonstrate that McMillan satisfied his burden.
1295: Whether the agency carried its burden to show it would have denied the tour extension absent protected military service
For all of the reasons explained, the DEA failed to demonstrate that it would have made the same decision in the absence of McMillan's military service.
1323: USERRA section 4311(a) discrimination: whether the Blackberry placement and OPR investigation denied a 'benefit of employment' based on military service

We agree with the Board, however, that the agency's alleged placement of the Blackberry in Mr. Kitlinski's car did not constitute the denial of a "benefit of employment" within the meaning of section 4311(a) of USERRA.
1324: USERRA section 4311(a) hostile work environment based on military status/anti-military animus: claim rejected for lack of any allegation of military-based motivation
The discrimination claim in the form of a hostile work environment based on military status therefore fails on that ground.
1325: USERRA section 4311(b) anti-retaliation: whether the Blackberry incident and OPR investigation were discrimination in employment or adverse employment actions

We therefore sustain the Board's ruling that Mr. Kitlinski failed to make a nonfrivolous allegation that the discrete actions about which he complains—the Blackberry incident and the investigative activities that followed—violated USERRA's anti-retaliation provision.
1342: USERRA discrimination and retaliation claims based on veteran status and prior USERRA claims in a non-selection; Board found no evidence of motivating or substantial factor and affirmed.
The record evidence merely shows that HHS found Mr. Jones unqualified based on his lack of requisite experience.
1384: USERRA discrimination claim: whether military service was a substantial or motivating factor in the non-selection for the Health System Administrator position; Board's denial affirmed as supported by substantial evidence.
we conclude that the Board's order dismissing Mr. Jones's discrimination claims is supported by substantial evidence.
1385: USERRA retaliation claim under 38 U.S.C. § 4311(b) based on prior VEOA litigation; Board's denial affirmed as supported by substantial evidence.
The Board relied on the evidence to determine that the AFRH did not retaliate against Mr. Jones. Because the Board's determination was supported substantial evidence, we affirm.
1460: VEOA veterans' preference claim: the Board's finding that the applicant's right to compete under VEOA was not violated in the hiring process was affirmed.
we conclude that substantial evidence supports the Board's determination that Ms. McMillon's VEOA right to compete was not violated.
1474: VEOA claim that HHS failed to credit preference-eligible veteran's experience in applications for four positions; court held the agency considered all experience and the Board's findings were supported by substantial evidence.
We conclude that the Board's decisions in these two cases are supported by substantial evidence.
1664: USERRA discrimination claim based on security clearance revocation; Board lacked authority to review clearance revocation under Egan and the USERRA claim failed; discrimination/reprisal defense tied to clearance revocation not reviewable
Congress has not "specifically . . . provided otherwise" in this case, because USERRA makes no mention of security clearances, explicitly or otherwise.
1665: USERRA reemployment claim under 38 U.S.C. 4312 after return to work and later termination for alleged antimilitary animus; no actionable reemployment claim

But when an employee has returned to employment and is subsequently terminated due to antimilitary animus, no claim exists under § 4312, even if a claim for discrimination under § 4311 might otherwise be available.
2023: VEOA veterans' preference claim: the Board sustained the agency's finding that the preference-eligible veteran was not qualified for the vacant position, so no right-to-compete violation occurred.
On this record, we do not believe that the Board's determination was arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or not in accordance with law, and it was supported by substantial evidence.
2036: Veterans' preference remedy: Board's order that DHHS reconstruct the selection process with Russell's correct 10-point preference, which the court upheld as appropriate where it was uncertain whether he would have been selected.
We find no fault in the Board's determination that such an uncertainty existed.
2037: Veterans' preference: whether the Board should have required an OPM pass-over audit under 5 U.S.C. § 3318 rather than an agency explanation; court held no audit was required because Russell was not among the three highest-ranking eligible candidates.

We disagree. Under 5 U.S.C. § 3318, if Mr. Russell had been one of the three highest-ranking eligible candidates, then such an audit would have been necessary before DHHS could select a lower-ranking applicant.
2038: Veterans' preference (VEOA) merits: substantial evidence supported the finding that Russell was not qualified for the position (minimum education and specialized experience not met), so VEOA does not require his consideration.
Here, the agency's decision finding Mr. Russell unqualified is supported by substantial evidence.
2124: USERRA discrimination: whether Jones's military service was a substantial or motivating factor in his non-selection, and whether HHS would have made the same selection anyway
substantial evidence supports the Board's conclusion that Jones had not established that his military service was a "substantial or motivating factor" in his non-selection.
2125: USERRA retaliation: whether the non-selection was retaliation for Jones's prior suits against HHS hiring decisions
Substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that the HHS actions taken in this case were not in retaliation.
2126: VEOA veterans' preference claim: veteran preferences do not apply to merit-process appointments, and Jones was allowed to compete
Therefore, we conclude that the appellant's VEOA claims are groundless.
2247: VEOA and USERRA merits: the Board properly found no veterans' preference violation and no discrimination or retaliation for non-selection, based on credited testimony and a supported finding of lack of qualifications.
Mr. Jones does not point to any evidence showing that his VEOA rights were violated in the course of the agency's selection process.
2389: VEOA veterans' preference claim: whether the FDIC violated Miller's veterans' preference or right to compete when it cancelled the vacancy and he was not selected; Board found no violation and the court affirmed.
We discern no reversible error in the Board's ruling that VEOA violation was not shown.
2512: VEOA veterans' preference claim over nonselection for a merit promotion position; Board denied relief on the merits and the court affirmed.
The Board correctly applied the law to Mr. Barry's VEOA claim and substantial evidence supports its underlying findings.
2612: Whether placing the Recent Graduate position in the excepted service under the Pathways Recent Graduates Program violated the veterans' preference statute §3302(1); held the President validly excepted the position under §3302(1) and OPM regulations.

we conclude that the President acted within the authority Congress granted him in § 3302(1) to create the Recent Graduates Program and except positions from the competitive service to fulfill the goals of the program.
2613: Whether the recent-graduate eligibility requirement (minimum educational requirement) violated §§3308 and 3320; held OPM's implementing regulations permissible under Chevron and no violation occurred.
We find no conflict between OPM’s regulations and Congress’s intent expressed in §§ 3308 and 3320.
2618: USERRA discrimination: whether McDermott's military service was a motivating factor in USPS's failure to recognize his preference-eligible veteran status (clerical error); Board found no discriminatory motivation and the court affirmed under substantial evidence review.
We find that that the Board's determination is supported by substantial evidence.
2619: USERRA discrimination: whether McDermott's military service was a motivating factor in USPS's decision to place him on enforced leave; Board found no discriminatory motivation and the court affirmed.
Nothing in the record suggests that Mr. McDermott's military service was a motivating factor in any of USPS's actions to place Mr. McDermott on enforced leave.
2893: USERRA discrimination claim: whether the agency denied Hayden a position upgrade (a benefit of employment) because of his military service, including the burden-shifting framework and the agency's affirmative defense. Court vacated and remanded for further factfinding.
With respect to his claim of discrimination based on military service, however, we vacate the Board's decision and remand for further factfinding.
2894: USERRA reemployment claim: whether Hayden was entitled to reemployment at the GS-12 level under 38 U.S.C. 4312 and 5 C.F.R. 353.106(c). Court affirmed the Board's denial.
As such, we affirm the Board's decision with respect to Hayden's reemployment claim.
2895: USERRA retaliation claim under 38 U.S.C. 4311(b) based on Hayden's consultation with ESGR. Court affirmed the Board's finding that Hayden failed to meet his burden.
Given these factfindings, substantial evidence supports the Board's conclusion that Hayden failed to meet his burden with respect to retaliation.
2921: VEOA claim that the Air Force denied Dean the chance to compete for a criminal investigator position and failed to give him veterans' preference; the court held the position was excepted service and the PAQ process did not violate veterans' preference rules.
Therefore, as Mr. Dean has failed to carry his burden, we affirm the decision of the MSPB.
3024: Veterans' preference under VEOA: whether the agency complied with the DoDI requirement to select a preference-eligible veteran over an equally well qualified candidate; the court held Bazan was not equally well qualified and affirmed denial of the VEOA claim.
Under any reading of the record, Mr. Bazan was not “equally well qualified” such that the Army must have selected Mr. Bazan over the selectee under DoDI No. 1442.02.
3114: VEOA veterans' preference claim challenging nonselection for a preference-eligible-only position; the Board properly filled the positions under MPP procedures, where veterans preference points do not apply, and the VA did not violate veterans preference law.
The Board determined that these Housekeeping Aid positions were properly filled by the MPP procedure.
3339: USERRA discrimination claim: employee failed to show veteran status was a substantial or motivating factor in her probationary termination, and the Board correctly required that showing.
We agree with the government that the Board did not err in interpreting the law to require proof of a substantial or motivating factor for a USERRA claim.
3539: USERRA discrimination claim: whether military service was a substantial or motivating factor in HHS's non-selection decisions; the court held the employee failed to meet his initial evidentiary burden.
Mr. Jones failed to demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that his military service was a motivating factor in HHS's decision not to hire him for the subject job vacancies.
5135: VEOA claim: whether HRSA violated Jones's veterans' preference rights by not crediting all material experience in its non-selection decision; the court found substantial evidence supported the Board's denial.
The Board credited the experts’ testimony, which is “virtually unreviewable” by this court.
5136: USERRA claim: whether Jones's prior military service or USERRA activity was a substantial or motivating factor in the non-selection; the court found no direct or circumstantial evidence shown and affirmed the Board.

We conclude that the Board did not err in finding that Mr. Jones failed to point to any direct evidence that his prior military service was a substantial or motivating factor in HRSA’s decision to not select him for the Public Health Advisor position.
5212: Discrimination/retaliation defense: claim that removal was retaliation for prior EEO activity rejected on substantial evidence.
Substantial evidence supports this conclusion, and we defer to the AJ's factual findings and credibility determinations on this issue.
5627: Discrimination affirmative defense: the Board found Boyd did not prove reprisal for prior EEO activity, and the court affirmed.
Because the administrative judge’s conclusions were supported by substantial evidence, we agree for the same reasons.
5921: USERRA discrimination claim: whether preference-eligible veteran status was a substantial or motivating factor in the agency's timing of McGuffin's termination, and whether the agency proved a valid reason and that it would have terminated him anyway. The court held substantial evidence did not support the Board's finding of no violation.

The record compels a finding that SSA's decision to terminate Mr. McGuffin when it did—four days before he completed one year of employment—was substantially motivated by Mr. McGuffin's preference-eligible veteran status.
7178: Retaliation for protected union activity under 5 U.S.C. 7116(a): substantial evidence supports finding that protected activity motivated the discipline (Letterkenny prima facie case and pretext).

We find that substantial evidence supports the Board's affirmance of the Hearing Officer's conclusion that Officer Konczos's protected activity motivated the USCP's decision to issue a Command Discipline Warning.
7511: USERRA discrimination: whether Broaden's military service was a substantial or motivating factor in his non-selection for the Air Traffic Control Specialist position; Board finding of no motivating factor affirmed as supported by substantial evidence.

Accordingly, we determine that the Board determination finding that Mr. Broaden did not satisfy his initial burden to show that his military service was a motivating factor in the FAA's decision not to hire him as an Air Traffic Control Specialist (MSS-1, Level 12), Support Specialist is supported by substantial evidence.
7512: Whether the advertised position requirements were discriminatory against veterans under USERRA; Board finding that the requirements were not discriminatory affirmed as supported by substantial evidence.
Nonetheless, we conclude that the ALJ's finding that the requirements of the advertised position are not discriminatory against veterans is supported by substantial evidence.
7591: USERRA claim that the FERS military-deposit requirement denied Faris a benefit of employment (FERS credit for LWOP military service without paying a deposit), and that the agency wrongly refused a deposit for April 2017 inactive-duty National Guard training. The court held no USERRA benefit was denied.
Accordingly, his USERRA claim fails, and the MSPB did not err in denying his request for corrective action.
7667: Disability discrimination: the Board rejected the claim that the agency failed to provide reasonable accommodations, and the court affirmed that finding.
These findings of fact are supported by substantial evidence.
7801: VEOA claim that ATF was required to make the appointment under its Veterans' Recruitment Appointment authority; the Board's denial was upheld.
We hold the Board correctly concluded that ATF was not required to make an appointment for the position in question under its VRA authority
7802: Whether the veteran was denied the opportunity to compete under 5 U.S.C. 3304(f)(1); the court held no denial occurred and veterans' preference procedures are not required for that opportunity.
Ms. Trimble was not denied an opportunity to compete
7803: Whether veterans' preference applies to a merit-promotion vacancy filled without competitive examination; held that no preference applied.
veterans are not entitled to a preference when the selection process being used is merit promotion
8205: Retaliation defense based on Grissom's civil RICO lawsuit under 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(9)(A)(ii): the Board found no genuine nexus between the lawsuit and the removal.
We thus affirm the Board's finding on this issue.
8414: Retaliation affirmative defense: Kolenc failed to prove his removal was reprisal for prior grievances and protected activity.
We see no error in the AJ's finding that Mr. Kolenc "failed to prove by preponderant evidence that he was retaliated against for engaging in protected activity."
8493: USERRA discrimination claim: the court held the Board failed to apply the Sheehan factors and vacated and remanded the USERRA assessment for additional fact findings.
We therefore vacate and remand this issue to the Board for additional fact findings concerning Santos's pre-PIP performance and Ms. Balles's motivations for instituting the PIP.
8529: Whether DLA violated the veterans' preference statute, 5 U.S.C. § 3311(2) and 5 C.F.R. § 302.302(d), by failing to credit a preference-eligible veteran's material experience in his application, where an automated questionnaire response made him ineligible and the rest of the application was not considered.
Section 3311(2) requires the agency to credit all experience material to the position.
8597: VEOA opportunity-to-compete claim under 5 U.S.C. § 3304(f)(1): Board's finding that the veteran was not denied a fair opportunity to compete was supported by substantial evidence, so the claim failed.
With respect to Ms. Trimble's claim that she was deprived of a fair opportunity to compete in violation of § 3304(f)(1), we hold substantial evidence supports the Board's finding to the contrary.
8598: VEOA veterans' preference claim under 5 U.S.C. § 3330a: veterans' preference does not apply to a merit promotion position, so the failure to apply it does not establish a VEOA violation.
we hold the Board correctly concluded the veterans' preference was inapplicable to the merits promotion position for which Ms. Trimble applied.
8788: USERRA discrimination claim over non-selection for a federal position: the Board found the veteran failed to show military service was a substantial or motivating factor, and the court held that finding supported by substantial evidence; USERRA does not reach veterans' preference claims.
Substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that Ms. Trimble failed to carry her initial burden to show that her military service was a substantial or motivating factor in her non-selection.
8994: VEOA veterans' preference claim: Board correctly found no VEOA violation where the veteran was given an opportunity to compete and the agency used merit-promotion procedures under which veterans' preference was not required.

Mr. Jolley has not shown a violation on the facts he describes: HUD accepted applications for the positions under both the competitive-examination and merit-promotion processes and ultimately chose to fill both positions under the merit-promotion procedure.
9293: USERRA discrimination claim: whether Moore's military service was a substantial or motivating factor in his probationary termination; the Board found it was not and the court affirmed.
The Board correctly denied Mr. Moore's request for corrective action because he failed to establish a violation of USERRA.
9331: Whether veterans' hiring rights under the VEOA (Title 5 veterans' preference) apply to VHA's appointment of a nurse practitioner, a position covered by 38 U.S.C. 7401(1) and 7403(a)(1); the court held they do not.
We agree that this case comes within that holding and therefore affirm.
9514: Discrimination claim: whether summary judgment for the Library was proper because plaintiff failed to show pretext for race, color, and national origin discrimination in non-selection (significantly better qualifications theory).

In short, we agree with OCWR that Ms. Leggett has not shown that there is a genuine dispute that the Library's asserted non-discriminatory reasons for passing on Ms. Leggett were a pretext for unlawful discrimination.
9572: Veterans' preference under VEOA: whether the Navy denied the veteran's right to compete, violated pass-over rights, or improperly filled the position through Expedited Hiring Authority procedures; Board denial of corrective action affirmed.
Nor did the Navy violate Mr. Williams’ rights by closing the position and filling it under its EHA procedures.
9738: USERRA claim standard: the court held the Board erred by requiring Adams to show military service was a motivating factor, because differential pay is available only to military members, so he needed only show denial of a benefit of employment.

Because differential pay is only available to members of the military, we agree with Mr. Adams that the Board erred in its legal analysis by requiring that he show that his military service was a motivating factor in the agency's decision to deny differential pay.
10024: VEOA opportunity to compete: Board affirmed that Jolley was not qualified for the Charleston FOD position, so he was not denied an opportunity to compete and the VEOA claim failed.
And "the VEOA does not enable veterans to be considered for positions for which they are not qualified."
10025: USERRA military-service discrimination claim: Board affirmed rejection of the claim because HUD rejected the application for lack of qualifications, not military service; dual announcements held not to violate USERRA.

The only evidence in the record provides substantial evidence for the Board's conclusion that HUD rejected Mr. Jolley's application because he lacked the necessary qualifications, not due to his military service.
10135: USERRA discrimination claim: the court affirmed the Board's finding that Beck's military service was a motivating or substantial factor in the nonselection, so the employee satisfied the first prong.
At the outset, we affirm the Board's determinations vis-à-vis the first prong of the USERRA framework.
10136: USERRA second prong: the Navy failed to show it would have hired Wible absent Beck's military service, and the Board's preselection determination was not supported by substantial evidence and could not save the Navy's decision.
We therefore conclude that, to the extent the Navy could establish that it preselected Wible, it nevertheless cannot disentangle its purported preselection from its USERRA-based discrimination.
10392: USERRA retaliation claim: whether supervisors' post-resignation job references were motivated by employee's protected USERRA activity; Board found no improper motive and affirmed
we affirm the decision of the Board.
10419: USERRA discrimination claim: whether Trimble's military service was a substantial or motivating factor in her non-selection; the Board's finding of no service-based discrimination was upheld under substantial evidence review.
Ms. Trimble's non-selection alone is insufficient to carry her burden to show a USERRA violation.
10759: USERRA discrimination claim: substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that military service was not a motivating factor in non-selection for the Executive Assistant position.
We affirm the Board's decision denying Ms. Trimble's USERRA claim because substantial evidence supports that Ms. Trimble's military service was not a motivating factor in her non-selection.
11154: VEOA right to compete under merit promotion procedures: Board's finding that the veteran had an opportunity to compete was supported by substantial evidence, so no violation of 5 U.S.C. § 3304(f)(1).
Because substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that Ms. Trimble had the opportunity to compete, we affirm.
11155: Veterans' preference claims: merit promotion listing does not carry open-competition preference rights, so no underlying preference violation supports a VEOA claim.
Thus, there are no underlying violations regarding veterans' preference that give rise to a viable VEOA claim.
11291: VEOA claim that the agency violated veterans' preference regulations and internal hiring policies (5 C.F.R. 302.101(c), OLC Memo 79-22); Court found no reversible error in Board's finding of no violation.
We find no reversible error in the Board's determination of no violation of section 3330(a)(1)(A).
11292: VEOA right-to-compete claim under 5 U.S.C. 3304(f)(1) based on failure to forward application to finalist panel; Court found no denial of opportunity to compete.
We see no reversible error in the Board's rejection of his right-to-compete claim.
11410: USERRA and VEOA claims of discrimination based on military service and veterans' preference: Becker failed to make a nonfrivolous allegation that military status was a motivating factor, and did not exhaust DOL remedies for the VEOA claim.
The Board correctly found that it lacked jurisdiction over Mr. Becker's VEOA claim.
11447: USERRA promotion reemployment claim: Board applied an incorrect legal standard by requiring the promotion to be automatic; vacated and remanded for application of 5 C.F.R. § 353.106(c).
We agree that the Board applied the incorrect legal standard and vacate and remand for further proceedings on Mr. Knox's promotion reemployment claim.
11448: USERRA discrimination claims (38 U.S.C. § 4311) on the within-grade increase delay and the promotion delay: substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that military service was not a motivating factor.
We affirm the Board's decision on this issue.
11764: VEOA claim: veteran's non-selection for merit promotion positions; court held VEOA guarantees only right to apply and compete, not preference in merit promotion, and agency did not violate VEOA
The Board was therefore correct to hold that Mr. Stewart was entitled to compete for the positions for which he applied, but was not entitled to point and ranking preferences.
11765: Time-in-grade requirement and special appointing authority under 38 U.S.C. § 4214: agency's discretionary decision not to use special appointing authority upheld; Stewart did not meet time-in-grade requirement
Mr. Stewart has made no showing that the DVA abused its discretion in declining to do so.
12011: USERRA discrimination based on uniformed service (anti-military animus): the Board found uniformed service was not a substantial or motivating factor. Court affirmed for the agency.
Here too, the Board did not err, and we conclude substantial evidence supports its finding.
12341: Whether 5 U.S.C. § 3330a(e)(2) barred pursuit of the VEOA claim while the parallel WPA claim was pending; court held the election bar did not prevent parallel pursuit of the veterans' preference claim.
Ms. Demery's VEOA claim concerns an alleged violation of veterans' preference rights, which does not prevent her from pursuing these claims in parallel.
12373: Whether 5 U.S.C. § 3304(f)(1) under VEOA protects veterans and preference eligibles who are current federal employees from denial of the opportunity to compete; en banc court held the statute covers current employees and overruled Kerner to that extent.
We conclude that the VEOA guarantees veterans and preference eligibles the right to compete regardless of their status as current federal employees.
12583: Whether veterans' preference opportunity-to-compete rights under 5 U.S.C. § 3304(f)(1) under VEOA apply to a preference-eligible veteran who is already a federal employee; court held the provision is inapplicable to federally employed veterans and affirmed the Board's denial of corrective action.
we conclude that the Board properly interpreted Kerner as holding that § 3304(f) is inapplicable to federally employed veterans.
12900: VEOA claim on the open competitive vacancy announcement: whether the agency considered the veteran's experience as required; court held the record supported the Board's finding that FDIC considered his experience, so no VEOA violation.
On this record, we cannot say that the FDIC violated the VEOA by failing to consider any of Mr. Burnett's experience.
12901: Opportunity-to-compete (5 U.S.C. § 3304(f)) claim on the merit promotion announcement: court declined to address the scope of Kerner and held that the consideration he received satisfied VEOA.

In this case, Mr. Burnett makes no claim that his application in response to the merit promotion announcement did not receive consideration from the FDIC, and the Board concluded that this consideration satisfied the VEOA in the context of the competitive vacancy announcement.
13286: USERRA discrimination claim: whether Santos's military service was a substantial or motivating factor in his removal under the Sheehan factors; Board found agency prevailed and court affirmed.
Accordingly, Mr. Santos fails to identify reversible error.
13327: Discrimination claim that § 8411(d) discriminates in favor of military personnel over OWCP beneficiaries; court held the claim rests on a misreading of the statute.
Thus, the Board did not rely on an erroneous interpretation of the statute in rejecting Mr. Macura's argument that § 8411(d) is discriminatory.
13346: USERRA whistleblower-type retaliation claim: Board correctly found Akerman did not nonfrivolously allege a USERRA-related protected disclosure preceding the agency action or that protected activity was a motivating factor.
Mr. Akerman fails to show that he nonfrivolously alleged that he made a USERRA-related disclosure at an earlier date, or that the agency retaliated against him at a later date.
13475: VEOA veterans' preference claim: whether the agency's reconstructed hiring process complied with veterans' preference rules, including the claimed bypass violation; Board found compliance and the court affirmed.
Upon review of the record, we see no legal or procedural error in the Board's decision and determine that it is supported by substantial evidence.
13527: VEOA claim: whether Schultz is entitled to lost wages and benefits under 5 U.S.C. 3330c(a) where he declined to participate in the reconstructed selection process and it is unknown whether he would have been selected.
Therefore, we agree with the MSPB that Mr. Schultz has not shown that he lost wages "by reason of the violation involved."
13528: VEOA claim: entitlement to liquidated damages for a willful violation under 5 U.S.C. 3330c(a), where no evidence of willfulness was presented.
And in any event, he has presented no evidence of willfulness as required by the statute.
13529: VEOA claim: whether the MSPB may award consequential damages, mileage, time and out-of-pocket expenses under VEOA; the court held no such remedy was shown to be available.
On appeal, Mr. Schultz has not presented any authority that the MSPB is able to provide such a remedy or that the MSPB erred in its legal conclusion on this point.
13698: USERRA discrimination claim based on combat veteran status: Board found no showing that military service was a substantial or motivating factor in the termination or leave restriction; applied Sheehan factors and affirmed.
We conclude that the Board's findings were supported by substantial evidence in both respects.
14539: Whether VEOA veterans' preference rights apply to VHA appointments of physicians under 38 U.S.C. 7401, 7403; court held VEOA does not reach physician appointments, so the claim fails for the agency.
Dr. Conklin's argument here runs headlong into that binding precedent.
14918: VEOA veterans' preference claim: whether the Navy violated Bumgardner's preference rights by selecting an equally preference-eligible internal candidate (T.R.) over him for an excepted-service attorney position
we agree with the Board that the Navy could not have violated Mr. Bumgardner's veteran-preference rights when it selected T.R. for the counsel position.
15175: Disability discrimination claim not reviewable in IRA appeal for lack of Board jurisdiction
the Board correctly concluded that it lacked jurisdiction over such a claim in the context of an IRA appeal.
